title: Question 9
stem:
Nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (NMRI) is used to obtain diagnostic information about internal body structures.

State, during the use of NMRI, the function of:

parts.label: (a)

markscheme_points.text: precession is about direction of m
frequency of precession depends or frequency of precession is in radi

hints: Hint 1: Think of each hydrogen nucleus (a proton) in the body as a tiny spinning magnet. What would a very strong, steady magnet do to the orientation and motion of all these tiny magnets?
Hint 2: Remember the motion is not a simple lining up. The magnetic axis wobbles in a cone around the applied field direction - this special wobbling motion has a specific name.
Hint 3: Focus on the frequency of that wobbling motion. What determines it, and in which part of the electromagnetic spectrum does it lie for the field strengths used in NMRI?
parts.proper_answer: The large constant field causes the nuclei (hydrogen protons) to precess about the direction of the field at the Larmor frequency, which is in the radio-frequency range.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Tiny Magnets in a Big Field**
Think of hydrogen nuclei in water and tissue as tiny bar magnets that are normally pointing randomly. When you put the patient inside the very large, uniform field, these nuclear magnets experience a torque and line up, but because they also have spin they cannot sit still.

Step 2: **Precession About the Field**
Instead of just aligning, each nuclear magnetic moment precesses - that means its axis sweeps out a cone around the direction of the large applied magnetic field, just like a spinning top wobbles around the vertical.

Step 3: **A Precise Radio Frequency**
This precession happens at one very precise frequency called the Larmor frequency. For the large fields used, typically about 1 T, this frequency is proportional to the field strength and lies in the radio-frequency (MHz) range. This is vital because a radio-frequency pulse at exactly this frequency can then cause resonance and flip the nuclei.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: If the Larmor frequency is set by the total magnetic field strength, what would happen to that frequency if the field is made slightly stronger in one part of the body than in another?

Hint 2: Think about why an image needs position information. How could a frequency that changes from point to point let you work out where a detected radio signal came from, or choose which slice of the body resonates?
parts.proper_answer: The non-uniform (gradient) field makes the total field and hence the precession (Larmor) frequency vary with position. This allows the position of the resonating nuclei to be located and the region/slice where resonance occurs to be selected and varied.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Making Frequency Depend on Position**
The large constant field alone would give the same Larmor frequency everywhere, so you would have no idea where any signal came from. Adding a small gradient field on top means the total field is slightly different at each position, so the Larmor frequency is now different at each position.

Step 2: **Locating and Selecting the Signal**
Because frequency now codes for position, the frequency of the emitted radio photons tells you where the resonating protons are. By changing the gradient, you can also change which slice or region satisfies the resonance condition for your fixed radio-frequency pulse, so you can scan through the body to build up an image.
